question.headline: Order status questions - cost problem or revenue problem?
question.asked: My business mentor told me it is easier to sell something that makes people money than something that saves them cost. I sell email agents that save cost. That offer is fully worked out, I know it inside out, and I have two live requests for it right now - it is only harder to sell. My market today is ecommerce, transport and wholesale, on cost saving. The alternative is helping sales managers quote faster and respond faster, which makes them money - but I would have to build the whole product, do the research, and rethink everything for a market I have never sold to. This is my business (Glimps, AI chatbots and agents for small and mid-sized companies in Belgium) and it decides where my revenue comes from. What do I do? Correction: my ecommerce clients are B2B, and in transport and wholesale most of the inbound is not quote requests at all - it is customers asking where their order is.

verdict.read: Then quote speed is the wrong number. In wholesale and transport the money is the reorder you lose when nobody answers, not the support minute you save.

quotes.text: you make another product and then within two or three years all of a sudden you have four mini businesses
not stop doing that. Like if it keeps working, you keep doing it.

call.heading: Sell orders kept, not minutes saved
call.text: Same agent, same three sectors, same where-is-my-order volume. Change what you count: not hours of support, but buyers who stopped reordering because they could not get an answer.

actions.do: Put a churn number on unanswered order questions
actions.how: Ask both prospects how many buyers stopped reordering last year
actions.detail:
A wholesaler does not lose the order he is chasing. He loses the next one. The buyer who waited two days for a delivery date remembers it the following month, and quietly places that order with someone else.

Rackham's move: ask how many accounts ordered less this year than last, and what an average account is worth over twelve months. Then ask how often those accounts had to chase for an answer.

That is the same agent you already sell. You are simply counting the loss on the right side of the ledger.

Keenan's move: the gap is not slow support, it is a customer who stopped trusting the answer.

actions.do: Keep the cost pitch for whoever feels cost
actions.how: Two numbers in one proposal, retention first, savings second
actions.detail:
Do not contort the product to fit your mentor's rule. Some buyers genuinely are buying a lower support bill, and telling them otherwise costs you the sale you already had.

Sandler's move: let the buyer pick. Open with the reorder question. If he shrugs, he is a cost buyer, so sell him cost and close him this month.

Belfort's point holds too: you can only sell what you believe. You have two live requests for a product you know inside out. Send both proposals with the retention number on top and the savings underneath, and let the market tell you which half they read.

dissent.text: Blount is blunter: status questions are a support problem, and dressing them as revenue is a story, not a product. Sell the cost saving and move.
dissent.full:
Blount thinks the bench is being clever. Where is my order is a support ticket. It has always been a support ticket, and a wholesaler who hears a churn theory attached to it will smell the reframe.

His position: you already have two people who want a cheaper support desk. Sell them that, take the money, and stop redesigning the pitch for a rule someone gave you over coffee.

The bench went the other way because the retention number is real and checkable, not invented. But Blount is right about the risk: if you cannot get the buyer to say the reorder loss out loud, drop it and sell what he came for.

verdict.vote_label: The vote — each adviser names who should make the call

last_reviewed.note: re-weighed: the inbound is order status, not quote requests

pn.label: What next
pn.sub: Copy a line into the chat

speeches.name: Alex Hormozi
speeches.text: Then you just told me the answer. Where is my order is not a cost question either - it is the reorder you lose. Same agent, same inbox, a different number on the proposal. Still nothing to build.

quote.text: you make another product and then within two or three years all of a sudden you have four mini businesses

speeches.name: Dale Carnegie
speeches.text: Carnegie's principle: talk in terms of the other person's interest. A buyer chasing a delivery date is not thinking about your efficiency. He is deciding whether you are easy to work with next month.

speeches.name: Jim Keenan
speeches.text: The gap moved. It is not slow quoting, it is a customer who stopped trusting that he will get an answer. The same agent closes it, but you have to name the right gap.

speeches.name: Neil Rackham
speeches.text: Ask what a chased order costs and you get a support figure. Ask what a lost account is worth over a year and you get a different meeting entirely.

speeches.name: David Sandler
speeches.text: Careful. Some of these buyers really are buying cheaper support. Qualify which one is in front of you before you decide which story to tell.

speeches.name: Chris Voss
speeches.text: Say it first: most people call us to cut their support load. Then ask whether any customer has quietly gone quiet on them. What comes back is your pitch.

speeches.name: Jeb Blount
speeches.text: Or you accept that this is a support product, sell it as one to the two people already asking, and get on the phone to thirty more.

speeches.name: Jordan Belfort
speeches.text: Whatever you pick, pick one and mean it. A half-believed revenue story sounds worse than a confident cost pitch.

conclusion.label: Where round one landed
conclusion.text: The bench dropped quote speed the moment you corrected it. The volume is order status, and the money in order status is the reorder, not the minute.

speeches.name: Jeb Blount
speeches.text: Alex, this is a support tool. You are attaching a churn story to a ticket queue because a mentor said revenue sells better.

speeches.name: Alex Hormozi
speeches.text: It is only a story if the number is invented, Jeb. Ask the wholesaler what a lost account costs him, and either the number is there or it is not.

speeches.name: David Sandler
speeches.text: Then let the number decide, not the framing. If he cannot get the buyer to say it out loud, he is selling cost, and that is not a failure.

speeches.name: Jim Keenan
speeches.text: The ticket queue is the symptom. If nobody diagnoses what the unanswered ticket costs, he is back to selling hours and wondering why it is hard.

conclusion.label: Where round two left it
conclusion.text: Everyone agrees the product does not change. The split is whether the retention number holds up in a real call - and that is answerable this week, not arguable.

ballot.why: It is a support product, sell it
The buyer judges ease, not efficiency
A lost account beats a saved minute
Qualify which buyer is in front
Two requests is still not a pipeline
Let their answer choose the story
Pick one story and mean it

ballot_note: The chair never votes for himself.
